hints: Count the longest carbon chain that includes the CHO carbon as C1, then identify the methyl branches on that chain.
walkthrough:
Find the parent chain including the aldehyde carbon**
Think of $\text{CHO}$ as C1 every time. Here the $\text{CHO}$ carbon is joined to a $\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_3$ group, so the longest chain through $\text{CHO}$ is 3 carbons long. That gives propanal as the parent.

Add the branches**
Carbon 2 carries two methyl groups, so you add 2,2-dimethyl in front to give 2,2-dimethylpropanal.

hints: Look at the starred carbon in C*=O, count how many sigma bonded regions surround it and recall what that means for shape.
walkthrough:
Count regions around the carbonyl carbon**
The starred carbon is joined to the central C, to H and double bonded to O. That is three sigma regions in one plane, with one p orbital left for the pi bond to O. Three regions means trigonal planar and $\text{sp}^2$ hybridisation.

hints: Recall which strong oxidiser converts an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid and why heating under reflux is needed rather than distillation.
walkthrough:
Link aldehyde to acid**
Reaction 1 turns $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCHO}$ into $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCO}_2\text{H}$. That is oxidation by [O], adding one O to the aldehyde group. The classic AS reagent for this full oxidation is acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

Choose the condition**
You want to keep the newly formed acid in the flask so it is not lost, so you heat under reflux to return any vapour and allow complete oxidation.
Final answer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heat under reflux

hints: Compare the functional groups in A, a carboxylic acid, and B, an ester, and decide which one can donate a hydrogen bond.
Identify the strongest intermolecular force available to the ester B which has no O-H or N-H hydrogen.
Relate strength of intermolecular forces to the energy needed to separate particles and hence to solid versus liquid at room temperature.
walkthrough:
Spot hydrogen bonding in A**
Picture $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCO}_2\text{H}$. The $\text{O-H}$ attached directly to $\text{C=O}$ is highly polar. One molecule can donate its $\text{O-H}$ hydrogen to the lone pair on the $\text{C=O}$ oxygen of a neighbour. That is strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding, even forming dimers.

See what B cannot do**
B is $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CH}_3$, an ester. It has polar $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-O}$ bonds so molecules attract by permanent dipole-dipole forces plus London dispersion forces, but with no $\text{O-H}$ it cannot form hydrogen bonds with itself.

Connect strength to state**
Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than dipole-dipole interactions. Far more thermal energy is needed to break the lattice of A, so A stays solid at room temperature while the weaker attractions in B are already overcome, making B a liquid.

Final answer: A has hydrogen bonding between molecules.
B has only permanent dipole-dipole and London dispersion forces between molecules.
Hydrogen bonding is stronger and needs more energy to overcome, so A has higher melting point and is solid while B is liquid.

hints: Remember NaBH4 acts as a source of hydrogen for reduction and that an aldehyde reduces to a primary alcohol with two [H] added.
walkthrough:
Write reduction with [H]**
$\text{NaBH}_4$ supplies hydride which we write as $[\text{H}]$. The aldehyde $\text{C-HO}$ gains two $[\text{H}]$ across the $\text{C=O}$ to give the primary alcohol $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. So S is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{OH}$ and the balanced equation is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCHO} + 2[\text{H}] \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{OH}$.

hints: Split the ester U at the COO link to see which acid part came from A and which alkoxy part must have come from T.
Recall the catalyst needed to speed up esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from ester U**
Look at U: the left side $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-C(=O)-}$ is clearly from acid A. The right side $-\text{O-CH(CH}_3\text{)}_2$ must come from the alcohol T by losing its $\text{O-H}$ hydrogen. So T is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$, propan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol.

Add the esterification catalyst**
Carboxylic acid plus alcohol to ester plus water is slow, so warm with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid which acts as catalyst and dehydrating agent.

Final answer: T is propan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$
Catalyst: concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ / sulfuric acid

hints: Recall what observation 2,4-DNPH gives with any aldehyde or ketone.
walkthrough:
Apply the carbonyl test**
Both X and Y contain $\text{C=O}$, so both give a positive 2,4-DNPH result. That is an orange to yellow to red precipitate of the 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone.
Final answer: X: orange / yellow / red precipitate; Y: orange / yellow / red precipitate

hints: Remember which carbonyl type reduces Fehling's solution to a red precipitate and which does not.
walkthrough:
Decode Fehling's**
Fehling's solution stays blue with ketones and with X, but Y gives a red precipitate of $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$. Only an aldehyde can be oxidised that easily, so Y must contain the aldehyde group.
Final answer: Aldehyde / aliphatic aldehyde group, $\text{-CHO}$

hints: Think about how many different groups must be attached to a single carbon for non-superimposable mirror images to exist.
walkthrough:
Define the asymmetry**
A chiral centre is a tetrahedral carbon with four completely different atoms or groups around it, so its mirror image cannot be superimposed, giving a pair of optical isomers.
Final answer: A carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups

hints: Deduce the aldehyde isomer with a chiral carbon by placing a methyl branch so one carbon has H, CH3, C2H5 and CHO.
Recall how to draw a pair of enantiomers using solid wedge for out of plane, hashed wedge for into plane, and straight lines for in plane.
walkthrough:
Find Y**
Y is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$, an aldehyde and chiral. The only fit is 2-methylbutanal: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CHO}$. The C2 carbon carries $\text{CHO}$, $\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$, four different groups.

Draw the mirror pair**
Draw the chiral C in the centre with two bonds in the plane, one solid wedge coming out toward you and one hashed wedge going back. In one enantiomer put e.g. $\text{CH}_3$ on the wedge and $\text{H}$ on the dash, in the other swap them so the two structures are mirror images and not superimposable.

Final answer: Y is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CHO}$ / $\text{CHO-C}^*(\text{CH}_3)(\text{H})(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)$
Two mirror image 3D structures with wedge, hashed and straight bonds around the chiral C, with groups $\text{CHO}$, $\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ correctly mirrored.

hints: Match the broad 3200-3600, the 1630 and the 1050 bands to alcohol O-H, alkene C=C and alcohol C-O respectively.
walkthrough:
Read the spectrum like a fingerprint**
No carbonyl band near 1700, but a broad band at 3200-3600 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ tells you hydrogen bonded $\text{O-H}$ of an alcohol. The 1630 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ band is $\text{C=C}$ stretch and 1050 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ is $\text{C-O}$ stretch, so Z is an unsaturated alcohol.
Final answer: 3200-3600 $\text{cm}^{-1}$: $\text{O-H}$ / $\text{RO-H}$; 1630 $\text{cm}^{-1}$: $\text{C=C}$; 1050 $\text{cm}^{-1}$: $\text{C-O}$

hints: Use the IR evidence to include one C=C and one alcohol group in a C5 skeleton.
Remember geometrical isomerism needs each C of the C=C to carry two different groups.
Add a methyl branch so the chain is branched yet the C=C is still cis-trans capable.
walkthrough:
Assemble the pieces**
You need five carbons, one $\text{C=C}$ and one $\text{-OH}$. A good fit is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=C(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{OH}$.

Check branching and E/Z**
The chain has a methyl branch on the double bond carbon, so it is branched. The left $\text{C}$ of the $\text{C=C}$ carries $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{H}$, the right $\text{C}$ carries $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, both pairs different, so cis-trans (E/Z) isomerism is possible.

Draw as skeletal**
In skeletal form draw zigzag lines for carbon backbone with a double line for $\text{C=C}$ and $\text{-OH}$ on the end carbon. Either geometrical isomer is accepted.

Final answer: Skeletal formula of 2-methylbut-2-en-1-ol, e.g. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=C(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{OH}$ (E or Z form accepted) showing branched C5 chain, one $\text{C=C}$ and one $\text{-OH}$

hints: Deduce X from the product (C2H5)2C(OH)CN, it must be the ketone (C2H5)2C=O, and mark the C=O dipole.
Start with attack of the lone pair on CN- on the delta positive carbonyl carbon while the C=O pi bond moves onto O.
Finish by showing protonation of the alkoxide intermediate to give the OH group, with a curly arrow from the O lone pair to H+.
walkthrough:
Set up X with its dipole**
The product $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{C(OH)(CN)}$ comes from adding H and CN across $\text{C=O}$, so X is pentan-3-one, $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{C=O}$. Oxygen is more electronegative, so label $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ and show lone pairs on O and on $\text{CN}^-$.

Nucleophilic attack**
Draw a curly arrow from the lone pair on $\text{CN}^-$ to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of the carbonyl, and a second curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ double bond onto O. This forms a new $\text{C-CN}$ bond and a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{C(CN)-O}^-$.

Protonation to the cyanohydrin**
Draw a curly arrow from the lone pair on the $\text{O}^-$ to $\text{H}^+$ from HCN (regenerating $\text{CN}^-$). This gives the final $\text{-OH}$ group: $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{C(OH)CN}$.

Final answer: X is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ with $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$
Step 1: $\text{CN}^-$ lone pair to $\text{C=O}$ carbon, $\text{C=O}$ to O to give $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{C(CN)O}^-$ intermediate
Step 2: intermediate $\text{O}^-$ lone pair to $\text{H}^+$ (from HCN) to give $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{C(OH)CN}$

hints: Consider whether NaCN is used up or regenerated when it supplies CN- for attack then HCN provides the proton.
walkthrough:
Spot regeneration**
A small amount of NaCN supplies $\text{CN}^-$ for the first attack, then reaction of the intermediate with HCN remakes $\text{CN}^-$. Because it is not used up overall it acts as a catalyst.
Final answer: Catalyst / provides $\text{CN}^-$ which is regenerated
